summary: Describes mechanisms to reduce the processing overhead of RSVP refresh messages, to remove the delay in recovering when a message is lost, and to keep reservation state without constantly retransmitting it.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP routers normally repeat full reservation messages to keep their state synchronized. This RFC defines ways to combine messages, identify them, acknowledge delivery, and refresh known state with shorter summaries.

questions: how to reduce rsvp refresh messages
what is an rsvp srefresh message

what is the rsvp message_id object
subtitle: RSVP extensions that cut refresh traffic and repair lost signaling messages sooner.

tldr.problem: RSVP repeatedly sends full Path and Resv refresh messages, so processing grows with the number of sessions. A lost setup or change message may not be repaired until a later refresh.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds message bundling, per-hop message identifiers and acknowledgments, and summary refreshes that name installed state instead of repeating the full messages.
tldr.outcome: The extensions reduce refresh work and can retransmit trigger messages before the next normal refresh. RFC 2961 is updated by RFC 5063.

today: RFC 2961 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5063. The RFC says its exponential back-off procedures should be reviewed against operational experience.

sections.title: The Cost of RSVP Refreshes
sections.content:
The Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) keeps reservation state by sending Path and Resv refresh messages between neighbors. Each session adds message generation, transmission, reception, processing, and memory work.

A lost message that changes state is repaired through later refreshes. Increasing the refresh interval reduces traffic but delays synchronization; decreasing it speeds recovery but increases processing. A lost PathTear or ResvTear can also leave resources allocated until the cleanup timer expires.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers repeat full messages so neighboring routers remember the same reservations. The repeats use resources, and a lost change may remain unnoticed until another refresh arrives.

sections.title: Trigger Messages and Refresh Messages
sections.content:
A trigger message announces new or changed state, including a new reservation, a changed route, or a changed object. A refresh message repeats state that was already advertised, with the same information and path.

Only Path and Resv messages can be refresh messages. The extensions treat these two kinds of message differently: triggers may need prompt delivery, while unchanged state can be refreshed with less information.
sections.plainLanguage: A trigger message announces a change. A refresh message repeats information that the receiver already knows.

sections.title: Bundle Messages Reduce Per-Message Work
sections.content:
A Bundle message places one or more ordinary RSVP messages inside a single message. Its header uses message type 12; a sub-message can be any RSVP message except another Bundle. Bundling is optional, and a node must still receive ordinary RSVP messages.

A Bundle is sent as a raw Internet Protocol (IP) datagram with protocol number 46 to a neighbor known to support the extension. The sender must keep each Bundle in one IP datagram and should limit the time messages wait to be combined. The receiver checks the Bundle and then handles each sub-message as if it arrived separately.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can place several RSVP messages inside one Bundle for a capable neighbor. The receiver separates them and processes each message normally.

sections.title: Message Identifiers and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
A MESSAGE_ID object labels a message for one hop. It contains an 8-bit Flags field, a 24-bit Epoch, and a 32-bit Message_Identifier. Together with the generator's IP address, the identifier distinguishes the message; the Epoch marks a reset of the identifier sequence.

A sender can request an acknowledgment with the ACK_Desired flag. The receiver can return a MESSAGE_ID_ACK object, either in another RSVP message or in an Ack message of type 13. A sender can retransmit a trigger sooner than the ordinary refresh interval and stop when it receives an acknowledgment. The receiver can also use identifiers to recognize refreshes and discard out-of-order messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier lets a router recognize a message it has seen before. When the sender asks for confirmation, the receiver can acknowledge it so the sender knows whether to retry.

sections.title: Summary Refreshes Name Existing State
sections.content:
An Srefresh message refreshes state by carrying identifiers from the trigger messages that created that state. It can refresh only state that was advertised with MESSAGE_ID objects. Different list objects carry identifiers for unicast and reservation state, or include source and group addresses for multicast Path state.

The receiver matches each identifier to installed Path or Resv state and refreshes a match. If state is missing, it sends a MESSAGE_ID_NACK; the sender then sends the full Path or Resv message. Srefresh must not let state time out, so its interval cannot exceed the normal refresh interval. The RFC suggests a default generation interval of 30 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: An Srefresh message names state that the receiver already installed instead of repeating the full Path or Resv message. If the receiver cannot find that state, it asks for the full message.

sections.title: Exponential Back-Off for Retries
sections.content:
When a message requests an acknowledgment, the sender retries it on a rapid retransmission timer until it receives an acknowledgment or reaches its retry limit. The interval grows by a factor of 1 + Delta after each attempt.

The RFC suggests an initial interval Rf of 500 ms, Delta of 1, and retry limit Rl of 3. These are per-interface parameters. Implementations must use the described procedure or an equivalent one.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender waits a short time for an acknowledgment, then retries after longer intervals. It stops when the receiver confirms the message or the retry limit is reached.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Nodes advertise refresh-reduction support with a capability bit in the RSVP common header. If a neighbor is not known to support Bundles or Srefresh, the sender uses ordinary RSVP messages and refreshes. A receiver that does not understand a MESSAGE_ID object causes the sender to retry the message without that object.

The RFC says these extensions raise no new security issues and refers to the security discussion in RFC 2205. It also notes that operational experience with exponential back-off, especially for multicast acknowledgments, should be reviewed before the document advances to Draft Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can fall back to ordinary RSVP messages when a neighbor does not support an extension. The RFC says its security issues are covered by the existing RSVP specification.
